title: Harness2: Google Research Repository Overview (2026)
summary: Harness2 is Google Research's new benchmarking repository for AI automation. Determine how it compares to existing workflow automation tools.
body_markdown:
## Harness2 was released by Google Research on GitHub


### What harness2 is


The repository describes Harness² as "a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing in an open world." **It keeps model weights fixed** . So it's not a new model you call by name.


It's scaffolding around an existing one, and that decides how you wire it up: there's no model endpoint to point a step at, only a framework to run and then connect.


An agent harness is everything wrapped around a model so it can act as an agent: the prompts it is given, the tools it can call, the memory it carries between steps, and the control loop that decides what happens next.


The model itself only predicts text. The harness turns that into something that plans, calls tools and checks its own work.


"Recursive harnessing" is the page's phrase for applying that idea to the harness itself, so the scaffolding is adjusted as part of the process. "Fixed weights" means the model is never retrained or fine-tuned.


Whatever improvement you see comes from changing the setup around the model, not the model. I haven't confirmed from the page how the recursion is carried out step by step.


> Whatever improvement you see comes from changing the setup around the model, not the model.


The page speaks of eight editable components. I haven't checked what they are, so I won't name them. In practice they are the parts of the harness you can change, and the article only relies on the count.


An executor is the runtime that actually carries out the agent's work. OpenCode is the default executor, and` --substrate cx` is the flag that switches to Codex.


Both OpenCode and Codex are coding-agent runtimes, meaning tools built to let a model read, write and run code. The practical consequence is that harness2 needs one of them available where you run it.


The three benchmarks behind the gains are LAB, WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench. I couldn't confirm from the checked page what each one measures, so treat their exact scope as unconfirmed.


Their names suggest lab-style and workplace or job-style tasks, but that is an inference, not a statement from the maker.


There is no release date to give you. The maker is Google Research, and the repo sits under the` google-research` organization on GitHub. The page presents it as new, and I won't guess at a date it doesn't state.


### How to get harness2 from GitHub


Clone or read it from the GitHub page above. Setup steps, requirements and licensing belong to the README, and I haven't confirmed them here, so check them before you scope any work.


For automation teams, the practical point is that no native integration exists. Reaching it from a flow means general building blocks, such as an HTTP request or an MCP step, pointed at whatever you host yourself.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) has no harness2 integration either, but a missing entry isn't a dead end there: its 742 integrations are counted straight from the open source monorepo, and roughly 60% of them were contributed by the community, not by the vendor.


So a gap like this doesn't wait on anyone's roadmap. Activepieces lets you have AI draft the missing integration and keep it in your own instance, so nothing depends on a vendor release.


Next comes what the maker's pages actually commit to, since that's what you'd be building against.
